extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, literary critics, students and theorists of humor/comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical criteria that explain why things are comic on stage and in everyday life — the archetypal mechanisms (e.g., transformation, repetition, snowballing) that produce laughter. Useful for dramatists, critics, and anyone designing comic scenes or jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: illusion_of_life + mechanical_arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY ARRANGEMENT OF ACTS AND EVENTS IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US, IN A SINGLE COMBINATION, THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core formal definition: a scene must simultaneously suggest a living continuity and reveal, within that continuity, a visible mechanism (strings, springs, gears). The stage is a privileged place for this because it magnifies and simplifies life, making the mechanical aspect legible. Use this as a touchstone when diagnosing whether a sequence or situation will feel comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation_of_person_into_thing
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughs arise when human beings are presented or slowly perceived as objects—e.g., Sancho Panza as a bundle, clowns becoming bouncing balls, actors stiffening into wooden dummies. Techniques: physical tableaux, exaggeration of rigidity, progressive dehumanisation. Avoid making the transformation gratuitous; the effect depends on suggestion and context that make the object-like reading plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual_suggestion_from_vague_to_clear
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of suggestion par excellence: start with vague, indistinct impressions and progressively solidify them so the imagination accepts the vision (analogy with hypnotic suggestion or falling asleep where shapeless masses coalesce into objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gradual gradation (rhythm, repetition, assonance, tempo) to lull the imagination and then present the comic image. Examples: rhythmic lines of Regnard that conjure a 'doll' image; Figaro's piling of epithets that suggest an animal. Anti-pattern: sudden, unsupported assertions of objecthood that the audience cannot be led into accepting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition_(jack-in-the-box_mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic repetition often embodies a repressed feeling that 'goes off like a spring' and an idea that delights in repressing the feeling anew: IN A COMIC REPETITION OF WORDS WE GENERALLY FIND TWO TERMS: A REPRESSED FEELING WHICH GOES OFF LIKE A SPRING, AND AN IDEA THAT DELIGHTS IN REPRESSING THE FEELING ANEW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition creates a mechanical cadence/tempo (crescendo, rebound) that produces laughter when it symbolizes automatism (Punch and Judy, Moliere: recurring exclamations, the tempo of a scene). Use increasing intensity and rhythmic recurrence; make clear what feeling is being repressed and what idea keeps repressing it. Avoid repetitions that feel purposeless or merely tedious—repetition must signify a mechanical inner struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack_(manipulation_of_characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic situation in which one character appears free but is actually a toy controlled by another (the dancing-jack); the spectator perceives the 'strings' being pulled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct scenes where an agent manipulates another's actions/opinions so the manipulated character looks like a marionette (Scapin manipulating Geronte/Argante). Personify opposing decisions or impulses as separate actors/voices so audience can 'see' the strings. Anti-pattern: failing to make the manipulator's control intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball_(cumulative_escalation_and_reversibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An initially small cause leads by arithmetical progression to a large, unexpected effect (rolling snow-ball); mechanisms are often reversible or circular so that effort may bring the story back to its starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chains of cause-and-effect that accelerate (toy soldiers, house-of-cards collapse, comedic property like a lost hat that keeps escaping). The circular/reversible twist (return to start) heightens comic effect (Labiche: eaten hat, La Cagnotte, Les Surprises du divorce). Avoid arbitrary escalation without connected causality—audiences need to perceive the mechanical linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting_mechanical_arrangement_behind_disproportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of proportion between cause and effect is not itself comic; what makes it comic is that it reveals a mechanical arrangement behind human affairs (contradicting life’s expected continuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a gag that relies on disproportion, ask whether the disproportion exposes a visible mechanism or automaton-like sequence; if not, the gag may fail. The page critiques simple formulas (Spencer/Kant) that reduce laughter to 'expectation ending in nothing'—the mechanical-structure reading is the critical ingredient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness_of_life_as_source_of_laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid mechanism occasionally detected in human affairs is experienced as an ABSENTMINDEDNESS on the part of life; laughter functions as a social corrective to that imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame comic incidents as revealing social or individual inattention/rigidity (coincidences, circular returns, automatism). Laughter is the reaction that singles out and represses this inelasticity. Use comedy to signal and remedy the 'mechanical' lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three_fundamental_processes:_repetition_inversion_reciprocal_interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Life appears as continuous, irreversible, and individual; their counterparts give comedy: REPETITION, INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE OF SERIES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these three as archetypal operations available to the comic maker: repetition (same situation reoccurs), inversion (order is reversed), reciprocal interference (series collide). Employ them singly or in combination to generate comic architecture. The page recommends studying them 'in their purity' to craft scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic_repetition_as_inner_duel_of_two_selves
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes repetition is not between two characters but within one (e.g., Alceste), revealing an internal oscillation between contrary impulses—one self wants frankness, the other restrains it—producing mechanical repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop internal contradiction as a 'mechanical' oscillation: make the audience aware of the two opposing tendencies so each repeated utterance escalates the tension until a comic release. Avoid portraying the inner conflict as wholly plausible mature ambivalence; to be comic, the two impulses must be inelastic enough to create mechanised repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical_repetition_of_complex_situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducing a complex situation multiple times (in different 'tempi' or with different groups, e.g., masters then servants) increases comic effect when scenes are complex yet seem naturally introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plays to repeat an arrangement across acts or across social levels (Ecole des femmes, George Dandin, parts of Amphitryon). The more elaborate and naturally integrated the repeated scene, the funnier it becomes. Risk: if repetition feels staged or forced, the audience will not perceive the comedic symmetry.
